Gynecology and urology · published research

Cyclical mastalgia

In one 80-woman trial, the study-defined response proportion was higher with laser than with bromocriptine plus evening-primrose oil, although both groups improved and the report did not establish laser superiority.

PBM Database summary

What the records report

In one 80-woman trial, the study-defined response proportion was higher with laser than with bromocriptine plus evening-primrose oil, although both groups improved and the report did not establish laser superiority.

Summary of the Evidence

One double-blind randomized active-comparator study examined low-intensity laser therapy in 80 women with cyclical mastalgia. It compared laser with bromocriptine plus evening-primrose oil over 20 days. No sham-light or untreated group, animal experiment, cell study, or independent replication was identified.

Human and clinical evidence

The authors reported a study-defined good response in 82.5% of the laser group and 63.9% of the medication group. Both groups improved from baseline on symptom measures. However, the paper described the measured reduction as greater in the medication group, while the laser group appeared to affect a wider sector of patients. The different response summaries make it difficult to conclude that laser was superior; the comparison is better read as a preliminary active-treatment result (Saied et al. 2007).

Animal evidence

No animal PBM study specific to cyclical breast pain was identified.

In-vitro and ex-vivo evidence

No laboratory or ex-vivo study directly addressing cyclical mastalgia was identified.

Treatment Parameters and Generalizability

The study used a helium-neon laser at 633 nm, which is red visible light, together with four infrared diodes. The wavelength of the infrared component was not clearly specified. The reported output was 15 mW, with treatment lasting 600 seconds per day for 20 days over a broad breast area. Fluence and irradiance were not reported clearly enough to calculate or compare a dose. There was no dose-finding comparison and no follow-up across later menstrual cycles.

Interpretation

This one trial found improvement in both the laser and medication groups and a higher proportion meeting the authors' response criterion in the laser group. The results do not establish a reliable advantage over medication or a PBM-specific effect because there was no sham or untreated comparison. Replication with validated pain and function outcomes is needed before drawing a treatment conclusion.

Evidence strength in source summaryVery low for symptom response compared with active medication
Publications and records1 article

Evidence strength rationale and next steps

One randomized active-comparator study reported a higher study-defined response proportion with laser, but both groups improved and the report did not establish superiority over medication. There was no sham or untreated group and no independent replication. A placebo-controlled trial using validated pain and daily-function measures across several menstrual cycles would show whether improvement is attributable to PBM.
